title: Flip a car's rear-view mirror to night with its tab, the housing steadied so the mirror's aim does not move
instruction: Switch the car's rear-view mirror to its night (anti-glare) setting without changing where it is aimed, then let go of it.
context: Flipping the interior mirror to night against the glare of headlights behind is something nearly every driver does. Owner's manuals: "Make this adjustment before you start driving and while the day/night lever is in the day position. Pull the day/night lever toward you to reduce the glare" (Kia); the mirror is aimed in day, and the night image is the same view only if the mirror has not turned. The tab sits on an over-centre hinge 38 mm below the ball joint the mirror hangs on and needs 0.10 N m (about 5 N) to go over centre, and its spring pushes the same torque back on the housing; this mirror's worn ball holds it with 0.07 N m. So a tab flipped with one hand tips the whole mirror (12 deg in the one-handed run) and spoils the aim; the other hand must steady the housing by its end while the tab is pulled, then both let go without nudging it.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Windscreen stand, fixed: a dashboard block (x 50 to 62, y -14 to 24, 18.5 tall); on it a section of 5 mm laminated windscreen glass 36 cm wide (y -13 to 23) and 38 cm along its slope, leaning back 30 deg from horizontal (60 deg from vertical) from its lower edge (x 52.4, z 18.5) up toward the robot to its upper edge (x 19.5, z 37.5), black ceramic band round its edge, two side brackets under its far half. (2) Day/night rear-view mirror (like CIPA CM32000, 10 in, wedge mount) on its stem from a button on the glass (x 29.9, y 5, z 31.5): housing 25.4 x 6.4 x 3.5 cm, black plastic with prism glass facing the robot, 180 g, middle at x 25.5, y 5, z 24; ball joint inside it 6 mm above its middle (turns at 0.07 N m). Day/night tab 28 x 22 x 5 mm under the middle of the housing's bottom edge, in day (pointing down, 15 deg toward the robot). Both arms start at the ready pose, grippers open. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Read every control step: the housing's turn from its start (about any axis), the tab's angle, and each finger's collision-hull points. 0 for the rest of the run once the housing has turned more than 1.5 deg (the view at the rear window, 2.5 m back, moves 13 cm). Otherwise: 0.2 tab moved 10 deg or more off day; 0.5 tab latched in night (30 deg or more off day: over centre, on its stop at 35 deg); 1.0 (success, held 1 s) latched in night, every finger point 1 cm or more from the housing and tab, and the mirror still (housing and tab each under 0.05 deg in 1 s). Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: a laser pointer at the driver's eye point lights the mirror; the reflected spot (bright in day, the dim one in night) is marked on a board 2 m behind and filmed: 1.5 deg of turn moves it 10.5 cm; the tab's position and the let-go are read from the video.
reset_notes: Push the tab back to day, check the laser spot is on its mark (re-aim the mirror by hand if not) and move the arms to the ready pose. Simulation: each trial starts the simulator afresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 20 Hz control. The ball joint is three hinges through one point, each with 0.07 N m friction (a worn ball; real ones are set by measuring the push that turns the housing). The tab's over-centre spring is a hinge spring that pulls toward the nearer stop, peaking at 0.10 N m (estimate). The few-degree tilt the tab gives the housing in a real mirror is not modelled; the tab's position is the device state. The clear glass collides but is not drawn.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms rose and pointed toward the mirror, then drew back near their bases; neither touched the mirror or its tab, which stayed in day); demo: 1.0
